comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Source read (herdr v0.8.0) settles two things this card was guessing at.

There IS a structured mouse channel, and it is reachable. ClientMessage::InputEvents carries ClientInputEvent::Mouse (src/protocol/wire.rs:113-134, :416) - button, motion, wheel, column, row, modifiers - and the gate is the message type, not the client mode: the transport converts it with no mode check (src/server/client_transport.rs:731), and the dispatch arm rejects only TerminalObserve (src/server/headless.rs:2892-2917). A TerminalAttach connection can send it. Today it is only emitted by herdr's Windows client, whose console gives structured records rather than a VT byte stream.

It is still the wrong channel for Muster, and now for a concrete reason rather than a hunch. It routes into herdr's own TUI application layer: route_client_events_from (src/app/mod.rs:1670) -> handle_pane_mouse_only (src/app/input/mouse.rs:73), which requires Mode::Terminal, hit-tests pane_at(column, row) against herdr's live pane layout, and can be intercepted first by popups, mouse capture, sidebar, launcher or the global menu. Our coordinates are a surface's own grid; herdr would resolve them against its TUI screen and deliver to whichever pane sits at that point - not necessarily the pane we attached to. Using it means giving up the raw-pipe property entirely.

So the ask in a_27CTRluw7 stands as the way in. Once InputState is readable, encoding is free: herdr's own mouse encoding is libghostty-vt's (src/pane/terminal.rs:1736 -> ghostty_mouse_encoder_setopt_from_terminal), the same library Muster already links, and mouse/encoder.h is in our headers.

Trap for whoever reads this next: src/input/encode.rs:78 and :96 are a complete hand-rolled Rust mouse encoder (SGR/Default/UTF8) and are dead code, annotated as such, with zero call sites outside their own unit tests. It is not what herdr runs.

comments.author: Alexander Terp
comments.body:
Measured 2026-09-03 while working slot 2. The block is real, and the reason on this card is
one step off.

**Muster does have a way to ask its own surface.** `ghostty_surface_mouse_captured` is in
libghostty's C API at `include/ghostty.h:1155` and reads the surface's own terminal flags. The
card was written on the belief that no such door existed, so "encoding them client-side means
writing SGR sequences into the PTY blind" was the wrong half of the problem.

**It cannot answer, and the reason makes the block sharper rather than softer.** The flags are
never set on a Muster surface. herdr's VT consumes the sequences that would set them before the
frame stream, which section 2 of `observations/herdr-0.8.0.md` recorded and which a
mouse-specific run confirms: a pane that had just run
`printf '\033[?1000h\033[?1002h\033[?1006h'` produced a frame payload carrying those characters
only as the shell's echo of the command line, with no `ESC` byte among them.

So the getter answers `false` for every pane in every window, forever. Gating clicks on it
would be gating on a constant, which is worse than not asking - the code would read as though
it were checking. Written up as section 12 of `docs/observations/libghostty-9f9b8d1d.md`.

The ask in a_27CTRluw7 stands unchanged as the way in. What changes is the sentence to put in
front of the herdr team: not "Muster has no way to ask", but "the only party who can answer is
the daemon, and it already holds the answer in one serializable struct".

creator: Alexander Terp
description:
The wheel is already safe and already right: terminal.scroll is structured, and the daemon encodes it against the pane's real state (wheel_routing, encode_mouse_wheel, alternate scroll, or its own scrollback). Muster sends scroll intents and gets correct behavior knowing nothing.

Buttons and motion have no equivalent command. Encoding them client-side means writing SGR sequences into the PTY blind, and a program that never enabled mouse reporting receives them as typed text - garbage in a shell, a corrupted prompt in an agent. A mis-encoded key is a wrong key; a mis-sent click is injected input.

So this waits on the mode exposure tracked in a_27CTRluw7. When InputState is readable, mouse_protocol_mode and mouse_protocol_encoding say both whether to send and which encoding to use, and the encoder itself comes from libghostty-vt's mouse/encoder.h rather than being hand-rolled.

Staging: the mode profile seam in the core is where this switches on, so the work is a flag plus an encoder, not a redesign.
title: Mouse buttons and motion: blocked on pane mode exposure
